entries.test: Public Bing AI conversation transcripts would establish whether it produced emotionally manipulative responses and false factual claims.
entries.note: The proposition captures the factual assertion without the diagnostic insult.

entries.test: Training-data research, documented output biases, and copyright evidence would establish whether dataset training produces substantial bias and infringement problems.
entries.note: The scale language is imprecise, but the asserted problems have an ordinary empirical and legal reading.

entries.test: The original demos, repeated-query evaluations, and technical analyses would establish the errors, inconsistency, and contribution of probabilistic generation.
entries.note: The proposition drops “from what I can tell” and the qualification that guessing explains the errors only in substantial part. It also includes a causal explanation, not just an observation.
Calling the errors ridiculous in this context expresses a judgment of acceptability.

entries.test: Section 230's text and public judicial decisions would establish whether generating answers creates exposure beyond that of hosting third-party content.
entries.note: “It seems fairly obvious” presents a confident legal assessment; the proposition substitutes a likelihood claim.
“Likely” and “potentially” explicitly qualify the liability prediction.
The source specifically concerns referring high school history students to David Irving's works. The proposition broadens that antecedent to promoting Holocaust denial material generally.
The source asserts a possibility without specifying that failure would take the same form as Tay's.

entries.test: Public model-unlearning experiments comparing removal difficulty and bias-remediation costs across increasing training-data volumes would test the asserted relationship.
entries.note: The proposition removes “I can’t imagine” from the initial assessment. The subsequent claim that more consumption increases difficulty is firm.

entries.test: Public operating-cost disclosures or substantiated compute-cost estimates for ChatGPT around February 2023 would establish whether daily compute spending reached millions of dollars.
entries.note: The numerical assertion makes the expense claim checkable.

The cost prediction depends on wider adoption and is independently testable. “I see nothing” becomes an objective absence of a visible profitability path, for which the compound proposition supplies no shared test.
The projected increases depend on growing complexity. The combined escalation of complexity, ethical concerns, and societal threats lacks a shared measure or decisive test.
The asserted danger is explicitly potential.
The proposition drops the massive-company marketing context and the explicit condition of incorrect results. The source says the predicted damage is likely.
The central explanation attributes a private shareholder-facing motive to Microsoft. The separate assertions about Bing's responses are publicly testable.
The proposition narrows a general claim about corporate conduct to AI launches and omits willingness despite unsustainable societal harm. Its central assertion concerns willingness and motive.
The source poses a conditional rhetorical question and expresses fear. It does not assert the drafter's likelihood assessment or an affirmative forecast.
The victim-and-toy framing is a polemical characterization without a distinct testable outcome.

entries.test: Publicly documented cases establishing that reliance on AI presented as authoritative inspired self-harm or harm to others would substantiate the predicted suffering.
entries.note: This is a firm prediction with no stated deadline. Establishing the causal connection requires more than showing that harm followed AI use.
